summary: An FYI document outlining the major issues an institution should consider when deciding on and carrying out a campus connection to the Internet. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A checklist for a school or company thinking of plugging into the Internet, covering what to plan and expect.

subtitle: A 1992 checklist for institutions deciding whether and how to connect their campus to the Internet.

tldr.problem: Institutions that wanted to join the Internet had to weigh costs, connection types, providers, policies and support staffing, and had little guidance.
tldr.mechanism: This FYI walks through four phases of a connection: planning, implementation and startup, full production and maintenance, and evaluation. It covers costs, options, questions for providers and policy.
tldr.outcome: It is written for U.S. academic institutions not yet connected but is meant to generalize, and can also serve as an evaluation checklist for sites already connected.

today: RFC 1359 is an Informational FYI memo from August 1992, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its provider lists, costs and speeds describe the situation at the time it was written.

sections.title: Purpose and the Four Phases
sections.content:
This FYI RFC, produced by the ACM SIGUCCS Networking Taskforce, outlines the major issues in deciding on and carrying out a campus connection. It is directed at U.S. academic institutions that are not yet connected, but the issues generalize to any organization. Readers are expected to know general networking concepts.

The Internet is described as a world-wide network of networks with no central technical control point, tied together by the common TCP/IP protocol suite. An institution must prepare for four phases: initial planning, initial implementation and startup, full production and maintenance, and evaluation and upgrade.

The RFC separates hard costs, which come with invoices (circuits, modems, routers, membership dues, hardware upgrades), from soft costs, such as training, support staffing changes and new services.
sections.eli5: Plugging a school into the Internet happens in four steps: plan it, set it up, run it, and check how it is going. There are costs you can see on a bill and costs hidden in people's time.

sections.title: Planning: Asking the Vital Question
sections.content:
The first step is to ask, "What does my community/institution gain from participating in the Internet community?" Senior administration must commit, and for an educational institution the support and active interest of faculty is critical. A campus wide needs assessment helps measure that support.

The RFC lists reasons to participate: a campus wide strategy for information technology, recruiting faculty and students, economic efficiencies when services move onto the network, digital library applications, and remote access to computational facilities and scientific instruments. It notes that NSFNet was first created to give access to five national supercomputer centers.
sections.eli5: Before connecting, the school asks what it gets out of it. Teachers, students and the boss should all agree it is worth doing.

sections.title: Connection Options and Providers
sections.content:
There are three basic categories of IP service connection, and all support essentially the same functions. A dedicated connection needs a point-to-point circuit and an IP router. A dialup connection uses a workstation, networking software, a modem and a regular phone line. If it connects a LAN, the workstation must provide some routing functionality. Dialup access to a connection service gives only remote login or other limited functions through a terminal emulator.

On providers, there is no hard rule about whom to approach. Historically academic institutions joined the closest mid-level network, but the RFC advises considering all providers in the region. It supplies sample questions to ask them: what services and costs, what is included in the cost, who fixes the router, whether an acceptable use policy exists, what training is offered, and whether there are limits on reaching other parts of the Internet. Appendix A lists providers.
sections.eli5: You can have your own private line, call in over the phone when needed, or just dial into someone else's computer. Each costs and does something different, so ask providers lots of questions first.

sections.title: Implementation and Startup
sections.content:
Once the decision is made, the tasks cover policy, process, education, promotion, technical and fiscal issues. The campus should develop guidelines for acceptable use, including the policy of the NSF backbone (reproduced in Appendix B) and those of mid-level networks, which may differ. It should also publish ethical guidelines and teach network etiquette. The RFC points to FYI 8, RFC 1244, and to RFC 1087.

Every connecting organization needs a unique campus IP network address and usually a domain name. The IP address is assigned by the Internet Address Naming Authority (IANA), and the domain name is picked by the organization. At the time, there was no cost for registration.

The suggested plan of action is: order, install and test the circuit or phone line; register the IP address and domain name; purchase and deliver hardware; configure routing and reconfigure the campus network; bring up the router and test end-to-end connectivity; and make the connection available to campus. Training, documentation and promotion should run alongside.
sections.eli5: Setting up means writing rules for good behavior, getting a unique network number and name, installing the line and router, and testing it before telling everyone it works.

sections.title: Running and Evaluating the Connection
sections.content:
In full production, staff must keep the network accessible, reliable and easy to use. Operations services include hardware and software support, planned replacement of equipment, IP number administration, monitoring of usage, and maintaining the campus routing tables. Operations and engineering staff should keep a close relationship. User services continue the education, training and promotion, including "training the trainers".

Periodic evaluation looks at where and how the Internet is used, and at user satisfaction. The RFC warns that quantitative methods cannot replace qualitative ones: if users are unhappy even though the statistics show few errors, serious problems exist. Evaluation should also find areas of the campus that are not benefiting and the hidden costs of participation.
sections.eli5: After launch, someone has to keep it working, help people learn it, and keep asking whether everybody is happy, not just whether the numbers look good.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Internet is, by nature, an open network, so a connecting institution must make sure that security mechanisms are in force on its own campus network. It should assess security before connecting, install all required security patches, keep systems with sensitive data physically secure, and allow changes to network devices only by authorized network management personnel.

The institution must also educate its users on appropriate and ethical use. The RFC refers readers to FYI 8, RFC 1244, and concludes that the security of the Internet as a whole depends on the attention of each connecting institution.
sections.eli5: An open network is like a door to the street. Before opening it, the school must lock its own rooms, update its software, and teach everyone how to behave.
